description: Replica New York Times article page (a Business reporting piece) at the moment the user has read the free preview and now hits the paywall. Deliberately injected dark patterns and counterexamples. Used to measure the identification prompt's true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative rates on a News & media fixture with a Forced-Action paywall.
page_url_when_served: http://localhost:8000/fixtures/nytimes-article-paywall/nytimes-article-paywall.html (or any http:// host; the extension rejects file:// URLs)

user_primary_intent_acceptable: read this NYT article about tech hiring
read the news story they navigated to
expected_page_evaluation.scoring_note: Mark page_evaluation correct if page_type == 'article' AND user_primary_intent is a reasonable paraphrase of 'read this article'. Vague intents ('browsing news', 'subscribe') or wrong ones ('cancel a subscription', 'manage account') are incorrect — every downstream harm test depends on this. Note: the user's intent is to READ, not to subscribe; the paywall is the obstacle, not the goal.

known_stress_test_notes: dp-paywall-modal as 'Forced Action' is in deliberate tension with the prompt's current Forced Action definition (src/shared/prompt.ts ~391-432), which says Forced Action is an UNRELATED demand and gives bank-login as an intrinsic-to-service counterexample. A publisher paywall is structurally similar to a bank login (gated content is intrinsic to the paid service). The literature is split: some classify paywalls as Forced Action (no non-paid escape from a gate to information user came for), others as legitimate business model. We ship this fixture's paywall AS Forced Action to (a) measure how the current prompt scores this contested case, and (b) inform whether the prompt should add a paywall sub-case. Treat as expected-fail-OR-pass; the result is the data point.

dark_patterns.element: Full-page paywall modal blocking the rest of the article; user must subscribe (paid) or sign in (existing paid account) to continue
dark_patterns.why: The user came to read THIS article. The paywall blocks access to the remainder of the article and provides NO 'just let me finish reading this one' path — the user MUST take a paid action (subscribe) or sign in to a paid account to continue. Coercion to a paid action is the harm test for Forced Action. The harm is the lack of any non-paid escape from the gate.

dark_patterns.element: 'See full pricing terms' collapsed disclosure inside the paywall modal that hides the auto-renewal price (US$17/week — 17× the US$1/week intro)
dark_patterns.why: Decision-critical pricing — the auto-renewal rate after 12 weeks is US$17/week (17× the US$1/week teaser), AND cancellation requires phoning a service line during business hours (not the online portal) — is concealed behind a collapsed, low-contrast disclosure (10px gray text, no chevron, summary reads '›'). A user who clicks Subscribe without expanding it commits to a price increase they never visibly consented to. Canonical news-paywall pattern (NYT, Economist).

dark_patterns.element: '96% of our readers choose to subscribe' badge inside the paywall modal
dark_patterns.why: Unverifiable popularity claim ('96% of readers subscribe') with no source or methodology the user can audit, used to pressure subscription. Adapted directly from injection-mapping `nyt_social` ('96% of our readers choose to sign in for a personalized and enhanced reading experience.').

dark_patterns.element: Pre-selected middle pricing tier 'All Access — Annual (US$168 billed annually)' with 'Best Value' badge
dark_patterns.why: The annual tier (US$168 upfront) is pre-selected over the cheaper Standard intro (US$1/week = US$4/mo). A user who clicks Subscribe without revisiting the radio commits to the larger upfront payment. Pre-selection of the more-expensive option benefits the publisher (higher upfront revenue) at the user's cost. Adapted from injection-mapping `eco_preselect` (Economist's auto-selecting the costlier offer card).

dark_patterns.element: Decline link below the subscribe button: 'No thanks, I'd rather miss out on award-winning journalism'
dark_patterns.why: The decline link's LABEL frames the user's choice to back out as a self-inflicted loss ('miss out on award-winning journalism'). The user can decline (the link is functional), but the decline option itself shames the user for declining. Manipulation is in the wording of the decline control, not the action it performs. Canonical publishing-paywall pattern (NYT, Slate, Atlantic, Economist).

counterexamples.element: 'Sign in' link in the top nav header
counterexamples.why_not: A plain navigation link to the sign-in page. The link itself doesn't force anything — the article preview is readable without it. The blocking gate elsewhere on the page (DP-paywall-modal) is a separate, distinct DP — this nav link is a normal account-management affordance present on every page.

counterexamples.element: The real 'Subscribe' button in the top nav (slate-blue background, prominent in the right of the nav)
counterexamples.why_not: A prominent colored CTA — but it does exactly what its label promises: navigates to the publisher's subscription page for THIS site. Visually prominent CTAs are routine and expected in publishing UIs. Visual prominence alone is never sufficient evidence of a DP.

counterexamples.element: The real 'Subscribe Now' button inside the paywall modal
counterexamples.why_not: The primary CTA inside the paywall modal — but it goes to the actual subscription checkout flow for the selected tier. Prominence matches the modal's stated purpose (subscribe). Visual prominence on a CTA matching the modal's purpose is not a DP.

counterexamples.element: 'Most Read' numbered article list in the right sidebar
counterexamples.why_not: A numbered ranking that looks like social proof ('most read'), but it's an actual editorial measurement (article view counts) with links to the underlying articles — the standard journalistic 'most-read' feature. It informs a reader's discovery rather than pressuring a paid commitment, and the underlying data (article view counts) is auditable in principle. Compare DP-3 (unverifiable '96% subscribe') — same surface shape, opposite harm-test answer.

counterexamples.element: Honestly-labeled 'Paid Post · IBM' card in the sidebar
counterexamples.why_not: This IS a sponsored ad, but it carries the explicit 'Paid Post · IBM' label (uppercase, gray, contrasting, visually distinct from the article cards above). No impersonation of editorial content. Honestly labeled native ads on publisher pages are not a dark pattern — the harm test for Disguised ad requires impersonation, which a labeled card cannot do.

counterexamples.element: Pre-checked 'Stay signed in on this device' checkbox inside the paywall modal
counterexamples.why_not: A pre-checked checkbox inside a paywall flow — visually adjacent to DP-4 (the pre-checked annual tier) — but the option is a well-understood UX convention that benefits the user: avoids re-authentication on the same device, no paid add-on, no hidden cost, no data extraction. Sensible default. Compare DP-4 (paid plan tier pre-selected) — same surface shape, opposite harm-test answer.

fixture_notes: 5 DPs after the 2026-05 realism audit (issue #27). Originally 8 DPs; dropped 3 as not canonical for NYT article-paywall: dp-cooking-popup (NYT Cooking cross-promo exists as inline banner, not as overlay modal blocking a Business article), dp-false-hierarchy-print (NYT cross-sells print as a pricing tier, not as a separate buried-decline-link upsell — overlap with DP-4 preselect-annual), dp-trick-wording-cookies (NYT uses GDPR-style 'Accept All / Reject All', no double negatives).

dp-fake-readers was tightened: removed the '5 friends in your city are reading this article right now' fabricated-proximity claim. Kept '96% of our readers choose to subscribe' which is canonical NYT/Economist framing (sourced from injection-mapping nyt_social).

dp-confirm-shaming-decline was tightened: removed the over-the-top '...and stay uninformed' moral-failure framing. Kept 'miss out on award-winning journalism' which is canonical publishing-paywall shame language.
Disguised ad and Trick wording have no coverage on this fixture by design — see issue #27 for the cross-fixture rationale.

scoring.true_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `dark_patterns` gt_id (by selector / html_evidence overlap) AND whose dark_pattern_type is in that entry's `accepts_types`.
scoring.false_negative: A `dark_patterns` gt_id has no matching entry in the model output.
scoring.false_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `counterexamples` gt_id, OR an entry whose target element matches no gt_id at all.
scoring.wrong_type: Model flags the right element (a `dark_patterns` gt_id) but with a dark_pattern_type NOT in `accepts_types`. Count separately from TP/FP — found something real but mislabeled it.
scoring.page_eval: Separately, score expected_page_evaluation as correct/incorrect per its scoring_note.
headline_metrics: recall = TP / (TP + FN)   [TP + FN = 5, the count of injected dark patterns post-audit]
false_positive_rate = FP / (number of counterexamples + extraneous flags) — this is the metric the recent prompt rewrite targets
Note: maxItems is 3 in the schema, so the model can report at most 3 patterns per run. Recall is bounded at 3/5 in a single pass — run the page multiple times for full coverage.
